title: TCS Wants Up to 8,900 Forward-Deployed Engineers. It Marks the Biggest Talent Bet in Indian IT's AI Pivot.
excerpt: India's largest IT services company is embedding thousands of engineers directly inside client operations and hunting AI acquisitions — a double shift that could reshape how Indian tech workers compete in the age of artificial intelligence.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • TCS plans to deploy 5,900 to 8,900 engineers directly within client operations.
  • Q1 FY27 revenue reached ₹72,275 crore, a 14% year-on-year increase.
  • TCS is shifting from organic growth to acquisitions in AI and cybersecurity.
  • Forward-deployed engineers will require deeper business knowledge and technical skills.
  • TCS's order book declined to $9.5 billion, indicating changing project dynamics.

Tata Consultancy Services has spent three decades perfecting one model: hire hundreds of thousands of engineers in India, train them on client systems, and deliver services at a fraction of what an American or European firm would charge. Now the company's chief executive wants to turn part of that playbook inside out. K. Krithivasan told Reuters this week that TCS plans to convert between 1% and 1.5% of its workforce — roughly 5,900 to 8,900 people out of nearly 594,000 — into forward-deployed engineers, or FDEs. These are not traditional on-site consultants rotating through client offices. The FDE model, borrowed from Silicon Valley companies like Palantir, means embedding engineers permanently inside a client's own operation, building and maintaining AI systems that sit at the core of the business rather than at its periphery. The announcement landed alongside a first-quarter earnings report that gave Krithivasan room to make the case. Revenue for Q1 FY27 came in at ₹72,275 crore ($7.58 billion), up 14% year-on-year. Net profit rose 4.7% to roughly ₹13,400 crore. The company added 9,279 employees — its strongest quarterly net hiring in four years — and AI-related revenue hit an annualised run rate of $2.6 billion, growing 13.6% sequentially. ## Breaking With Organic-Only Orthodoxy Perhaps more significant than the FDE announcement is what CFO Samir Seksaria said about acquisitions. TCS has been famously reluctant to buy its way into new capabilities, preferring to build from within. That stance is now officially over. Seksaria told analysts the company is actively evaluating acquisition targets in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and data security — domains where organic talent development alone cannot keep pace with the rate of change. > **"Net profit rose 4.7% to roughly ₹13,400 crore."** The shift is pragmatic. TCS recently partnered with Anthropic to give 50,000 associates access to Claude, the AI assistant, as part of a broader internal upskilling push. But training existing employees on generative AI tools is a different challenge from acquiring the kind of deep research talent that companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind are hoarding. An acquisition strategy lets TCS buy what it cannot grow fast enough. ![Silicon Valley — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg/3840px-Silicon_Valley%2C_facing_southward_towards_Downtown_San_Jose%2C_2014_%28cropped%29.jpg) ## What This Means for Indian Engineers in America The FDE model carries particular implications for the Indian diaspora's largest professional community in the United States. TCS is among the top recipients of H-1B visas, and a significant share of its American workforce consists of Indian-origin engineers on temporary work authorisations.
Shifting Strategy: From Organic to Acquisitions
›TCS is evaluating AI and cybersecurity acquisition targets.
›This marks a departure from TCS's traditional organic growth strategy.
›Acquisitions aim to keep pace with rapid industry changes.
Forward-deployed roles demand a fundamentally different skill profile than traditional IT services. An FDE is not writing code to a specification handed down by a client's internal team. They are embedded in the client's decision-making process, expected to understand the business domain deeply enough to design AI systems that create competitive advantage. That requires not just technical fluency in machine learning and data engineering but the kind of contextual business knowledge that takes years of proximity to develop. For Indian tech workers already in the US, the shift could open higher-value career paths — FDE roles typically command significantly higher compensation than traditional services positions. But it also raises the bar for new entrants. If TCS fills these roles with experienced engineers already on the ground in America, the demand for fresh H-1B transfers from India could soften at the margins, even as the company's overall headcount grows. ## The Order Book Tells a More Complex Story Not everything in the quarter pointed upward. TCS's order book for Q1 came in at $9.5 billion, down from $12 billion in the previous quarter. While management attributed the decline to normal lumpiness in large deal closures, some analysts noted that AI projects tend to be shorter in duration — lasting one to two quarters rather than the multi-year managed services contracts that have historically padded the backlog.
Evolving Role of Indian Engineers in the US
›FDE roles demand deeper business understanding and technical skills.
›Higher-value career paths may open for existing Indian engineers.
›Potential softening of new H-1B visa demand as roles evolve.
Krithivasan acknowledged this dynamic directly, saying that AI engagements create revenue unevenness because clients often want rapid proof-of-concept cycles before committing to full-scale deployments. The FDE model is partly a response to this: by embedding engineers inside the client permanently, TCS can turn episodic AI projects into recurring relationships. The broader Indian IT sector is watching closely. Infosys and Wipro have made their own AI-related announcements in recent weeks, but neither has articulated a structural workforce transformation as specific as TCS's FDE plan. If the model works — if clients are willing to pay the premium for permanently embedded AI engineers from an Indian services firm — it could set the template for how India's $250 billion IT industry evolves beyond the labour-arbitrage era that built it.
